puzzles.matchTitle: Drie seconden ruis, aan het begin van elk bericht
puzzles.title: Three Seconds of Static at the Start of Every Message
puzzles.scenario: Every message a space station sends to Earth begins with exactly three seconds of static, no matter who records it or which room aboard it comes from.
puzzles.solution: The comms officer taps the microphone twice out of habit before he starts talking, a tic left over from his time at a ground station where that was needed to wake the transmitter. It hasn't been necessary on the station in years, but the habit is so ingrained that no one even asks about it anymore.
puzzles.hint: Is the problem with the transmitter, the receiver, or whoever's pressing the button?

puzzles.matchTitle: Koffie die elke week een beetje kouder wordt
puzzles.title: Coffee That Gets a Little Colder Every Week
puzzles.scenario: The coffee machine on a space station has been brewing coffee a fraction colder every week, gradually, even though the machine reports no fault and the heating element checks out fine.
puzzles.solution: Since a new research module came online, the station draws more power during peak hours, and the coffee machine shares a circuit with it. A shrinking voltage margin is just enough to make the heating element work a little less hard each week, until an engineer finally traces it not to the machine but to the power budget.
puzzles.hint: Is the problem with the machine itself, or with what it has to share with the rest of the station?

puzzles.matchTitle: Een ster die knippert in een verdacht regelmatig patroon
puzzles.title: A Star Flickering in a Suspiciously Regular Pattern
puzzles.scenario: Astronomers spot a distant star's brightness flickering in a strikingly regular rhythm, enough to briefly hope for an alien signal, until the pattern is traced back.
puzzles.solution: A newly installed maintenance drone on the telescope's own support arm periodically crosses part of the aperture during its scheduled cleaning route, briefly blocking the starlight from that exact angle each time. The 'signal' didn't come from the star — it came from the observatory itself.
puzzles.hint: Don't look further into space. Look closer: is something sitting between the telescope and the star?

puzzles.matchTitle: Ze antwoordt voor haar naam wordt genoemd
puzzles.title: She Answers Before Her Name Is Called
puzzles.scenario: At the daily roll call aboard the station, one crew member always says 'present' a full two seconds before her name is actually called, every single day.
puzzles.solution: After years of service she knows the roll-call order by heart and knows exactly when her name is coming. She just answers a beat early out of sheer habit — there's nothing stranger to it than that.
puzzles.hint: How long has she been doing this roll call, and what would that do to her timing?

puzzles.matchTitle: Een sonde meldt zich, twee jaar later, vanaf de verkeerde plek
puzzles.title: A Probe Checks In, Two Years Later, From the Wrong Place
puzzles.scenario: A survey probe was declared lost after contact dropped during a severe solar storm. Two years later it suddenly transmits flawless data again, but not from the trajectory it was last tracked on — from a completely different course, never predicted.
puzzles.solution: The storm temporarily fried its primary navigation chip, leaving the probe drifting uncorrected for two years on backup power. Only once its solar panels had built up enough charge over that time for a full reboot did navigation and comms come back online, from a position that had long since drifted from the old prediction.
puzzles.hint: The probe wasn't lying about its position. The old prediction simply stopped holding after the storm.

puzzles.matchTitle: Twee identieke luiken, twee heel verschillende krachten nodig
puzzles.title: Two Identical Hatches, Two Very Different Amounts of Force
puzzles.scenario: A space station has two identical airlocks on opposite sides, always serviced and tested together. Yet one has suddenly become noticeably harder to open than the other, though engineers find no mechanical fault in either.
puzzles.solution: Given the station's current orbital phase, the stiff airlock has spent months sitting in constant, unfiltered sunlight, while the other stays in the station's shadow. The metal frame on the sunlit side has expanded a fraction from the heat, just enough to add friction, while the shaded frame has stayed at normal temperature.
puzzles.hint: Don't ask what's broken. Ask which side of the station gets more sun than the other.

puzzles.matchTitle: Elke week precies één eiwitreep te weinig
puzzles.title: Exactly One Protein Bar Short, Every Week
puzzles.scenario: The weekly inventory count in a locked storage closet always turns up exactly one protein bar short, though the smart lock has never been forced and only two crew members know the access code.
puzzles.solution: The newest crew member finds her ration too tight for her training schedule and quietly takes one extra bar each week, but restocks the closet the following week from her own personal supply, too embarrassed to just ask. At any single count it looks like exactly one is missing, even though it evens out over two weeks.
puzzles.hint: Is the bar actually gone, or does the problem lie in exactly when the counting happens?

puzzles.matchTitle: Berichten voor iemand die niemand aan boord kent
puzzles.title: Messages for Someone No One Aboard Knows
puzzles.scenario: For a week, a crew member receives private messages on his cabin terminal clearly meant for someone else, signed with a name no one aboard recognizes, full of detailed station gossip, until they suddenly stop.
puzzles.solution: A temporary maintenance contractor had linked her terminal ID to a forwarding rule pointing at her ground account before she left. When that ID was later reassigned to this crew member, the old forwarding rule stayed active by accident, until an administrator cleaned up the account list during a routine check.
puzzles.hint: Has this terminal ID always belonged to him, or did it once have another owner?
